title: Too Tiny for a Barcode! Why Tirol Choco Grew to ¥20 | Curio Archive
description:
That bite-sized Tirol Choco you grab at the convenience store register faced a shrinkflation uproar in Japan in early 2026—until the company posted a side-by-side photo proving it never shrank at all. Two sizes had existed for decades because back in 1993, Tirol Choco deliberately enlarged its 10-yen cube to a 20-yen single just to fit a convenience-store barcode—sparking a dual-channel strategy that now turns out roughly 600 million pieces a year.
For anyone who grabs a square chocolate at checkout and wonders about the retail rules hidden behind pocket-change snacks.

This episode begins in 1903 at Matsuo Shoten in the coal-mining town of Tagawa, Fukuoka, tracing how Matsuo Confectionery used a soft nougat filling in 1962 to cut cocoa costs and create the original 10-yen three-peak Tirol bar. After the 1973 oil shock pushed prices to 20 yen in 1974 and 30 yen in 1976, crashing sales, the company gambled on new molds in 1979—splitting the bar into a 2.5 cm single Coffee Nougat cube back at 10 yen, followed by classics like Bis (1984) and Milk (1990). As neighborhood candy shops vanished in the early 1990s, the 2.5 cm wrapper proved too small to print even a shortened 8-digit JAN barcode for convenience-store scanners. In 1993, Tirol Choco enlarged the cube to 3 cm, placed the barcode on its side, doubled the price to 20 yen to claim prime register space, and repurposed the old 2.5 cm molds for supermarket variety bags—explaining the February 2026 shrinkflation illusion that drew over 650 comments in one week. Finally, we uncover how Kinako Mochi broke out from a 2003 winter variety pack to sell 17 million pieces in five months, how the 2004 Akihabara spinoff (~50 staff) paired with the 45,600+ m² Fukuoka Tagawa factory (40-minute cooling lines, ~600 million pieces a year, plus an outlet shop) to launch 600+ flavors—including 2023's 34,000+ vote wildest-flavor poll winners Wasabi, Pizza, and Eel—alongside the 2018 Akihabara shop, 2022 fan festival, the September 2022 adjustment to 23 yen after a 29-year price hold, a ~40-yen fresh ganache line with a one-month shelf life, and the 2023 Vietnam overseas factory.

This channel has no affiliation with or sponsorship from any company or organization mentioned. All historical timelines, production figures, and sales data come from public primary and media sources listed below.

t001.text: That checkout Tirol Choco was wrongly accused in Japan.

t002.text: In February 2026, Japanese shoppers online claimed it secretly shrank.

t003.text: The brand clarified: two sizes always existed.

t004.text: Stranger still, it grew bigger for a barcode!

t005.text: While rivals feared hikes, it doubled its price to win the register.

t006.text: This Kyushu candy-maker treat now hits hundreds of millions a year!

t007.text: It started as a 10-yen candy-shop snack.

t008.text: Later, hundreds of flavors hooked picky adults too.

t009.text: Today, let's see how a 10-yen cube used barcodes to win checkout.

t010.text: Why did it stall? Look at its start.

t011.text: In 1903, in a Fukuoka coal-mining town, Matsuo's shop sold cheap sweets.

t012.text: As Matsuo Confectionery, that budget spirit lived on.

t013.text: In the early sixties, they got bold.

t014.text: Kids drooled over fancy chocolates behind shop glass.

t015.text: They were luxuries ordinary schoolkids couldn't buy.

t016.text: The second-gen boss vowed to make a 10-yen chocolate.

t017.text: Sweet dream, harsh math: cocoa cost a fortune!

t018.text: Pure cocoa at ten yen meant instant losses.

t019.text: With costs that steep, how could they hit ten yen?

t020.text: They stuffed soft maltose nougat right inside.

t021.text: Less cocoa cut costs and added chewy texture.

t022.text: Warm nougat stuck to teeth; they tweaked ratios.

t023.text: They nailed a crisp shell and chewy core.

t025.text: Named after Austria's Tyrol, it became Tirol Choco.

t026.text: Rich filling for ten yen—it flew off candy-shop shelves.

t027.text: Eleven years later, what storm struck next?

t028.text: The 1973 oil shock sent sugar, oil, and cocoa prices soaring.

t029.text: It doubled in '74, hit 30 yen in '76.

t030.text: Spare change to adults, huge to ten-yen kids.

t031.text: Sales plunged, nearly knocking it off shelves.

t032.text: How could they return to ten yen without losing money?

t033.text: Shrinking saved cocoa, yet new molds cost big.

t034.text: The boss gambled: retool to keep ten yen!

t035.text: In 1979, three peaks split into one cube.

t036.text: First came bittersweet Coffee Nougat in one bite.

t037.text: One-third the size brought ten yen back.

t038.text: That cute single cube sent sales roaring back.

t039.text: Even adults grabbed handfuls at old candy shops.

t040.text: Biscuit in '84 and Milk in '90 swept Japan.

t041.text: Then Japan's retail landscape shifted overnight.

t042.text: Candy shops closed as shoppers flocked to konbini.

t043.text: Its tiny saving grace turned into a flaw.

t044.text: The third-gen leader pitched convenience store HQs.

t045.text: After ruling candy shops, the team felt sure.

t046.text: Even buyers loved it—the deal looked all set.

t047.text: Then talks hit a brick wall: the barcode.

t048.text: Convenience stores scanned every item with barcodes.

t049.text: Barcodes need strict width and blank margins.

t051.text: Not even an 8-digit code fit—no deal!

t052.text: In 1993, it grew to 3 centimeters wide, with a side barcode.

t053.text: Avoiding the back fold, it scanned in a second—opening every chain.

t054.text: Bigger cube, double the price at 20 yen—why didn't it flop?

t056.text: Impulse buyers grabbed them easily at registers!

t057.text: As sales boomed, what about the old molds?

t059.text: Mini cubes filled bags with one outer barcode!

t060.text: Two tracks emerged: big singles and bagged minis.

t061.text: That solves 2026's shrinkflation myth right away!

t062.text: Older fans recall minis, thinking singles grew;

t063.text: Younger fans buy bags and think it shrank.

t064.text: Comparison photos drew over 650 comments that week.

t065.text: Still, how did registers alone hook adult collectors?

t066.text: The secret was 1962's layered filling design.

t067.text: Two layers with fillings became a flavor stage.

t068.text: With fewer kids, they courted adults early on.

t069.text: They packed classic Japanese sweets inside the cube.

t070.text: In 2003, a winter variety piece went viral.

t071.text: Kinako chocolate around chewy mochi tasted like wagashi.

t072.text: Amazed buyers urged them to sell it solo.

t073.text: When it went solo, how huge were sales?

t074.text: 17 million sold in five months—shelves emptied.

t075.text: After that hit, the Kyushu plant split roles.

t076.text: In 2004, Matsuo spun off planning and sales.

t077.text: Roughly 50 staff in Akihabara tracked every hot trend.

t079.text: Artisans tempered chocolate and fillings into molds.

t080.text: Forty minutes cooling, then wrapped—yearly output?

t081.text: This Fukuoka plant alone makes about 600 million yearly!

t082.text: An outlet next door bags slightly chipped pieces.

t083.text: Locals line up at opening, wasting zero cocoa.

t084.text: Tokyo ideas plus Fukuoka lines launch hits fast.

t085.text: Guess how many wild flavors filled this cube?

t086.text: Official counts now top 600 flavors in total.

t087.text: Limited runs rotate every three months like gacha.

t088.text: From tiramisu to boba tea, trends get cubed.

t089.text: They go bold too—even their own sales team objected.

t091.text: Top three: wasabi, pizza, eel—weirder sells more.

t092.text: They craft exclusive flavors for specific chains.

t093.text: Stores crave buzz; wild wrappers hook loyal fans.

t094.text: Mini wrappers act like art for binder collectors.

t095.text: So devoted, the firm hosted an event for them?

t096.text: 2022's fan festival drew over 100 fans to Akihabara.

t097.text: Fans pitched staff directly, turning ideas into snacks.

t098.text: Back in 2018, they even opened their first specialty shop in Akihabara.

t099.text: Turning coins into culture took fierce price discipline.

t100.text: Since 1993, singles held 20 yen for 29 years.

t101.text: With cocoa soaring lately, could that line hold?

t102.text: In September 2022, classics rose to 23 yen.

t103.text: Instead of just hiking, they pushed into luxury.

t104.text: Fresh ganache cut shelf life to one month.

t105.text: At nearly 40 yen, it proved adults will buy mini luxury.

t107.text: Three tiers beat inflation. Where to next?

t108.text: For its 120th year in 2023, its Vietnam factory opened.

t109.text: It boosts supply and brings Kyushu cubes across Asia.

t110.text: From Japan to Taiwan, we spot it at checkout.

t111.text: A century of survival rests on two sharp rules.

t112.text: First: cheap goods rarely die from tiny hikes.

t113.text: They die refusing to adapt when channels shift.

t114.text: Cling to old specs, fade with old streets.

t115.text: Second: upgrading never means scrapping old lines.

t116.text: Split singles from family bags; old tools earn again.

t117.text: Two channels reinforce a moat rivals cannot copy.

t118.text: Remember 1962's budget filling? Now a flavor stage.

t119.text: Turning limits into charm keeps old brands young.

t120.text: True classics evolve in step with daily life.

t121.text: Next time at checkout, see that cube's retail comeback.
